Distance and displacement:
Distance is the total length of the path travelled. It is a scalar: it has size only and is never negative. Displacement is the straight-line change in position from start to end. It is a vector: it has size and direction.

Both are measured in metres (m). Distance is greater than or equal to the size of the displacement. They are equal only for straight-line motion without turning back. A round trip has zero displacement. For two perpendicular movements, displacement = √(a² + b²).
Speed and velocity:
Speed = distance / time (v = d / t). Its SI unit is m/s. To change km/h to m/s, divide by 3.6. Average speed = total distance / total time. Instantaneous speed is the speed at one moment.

Velocity = displacement / time. It is a vector, so it has a direction. Objects with the same speed can have different velocities if their directions differ. Rearranged: d = v × t and t = d / v.
Acceleration:
Acceleration is the rate of change of velocity: a = (v − u) / t, where u is initial velocity, v is final velocity, and t is time. The SI unit is m/s². It is a vector.

Speeding up, slowing down, and changing direction are all accelerations. Slowing down gives acceleration opposite to the velocity (negative on a straight line). Constant velocity means zero acceleration. Rearranged: v = u + a × t. Free fall has a ≈ 9.8 m/s² downward.
Motion graphs:
On a distance-time graph, the slope equals speed. A horizontal line means rest, a straight sloping line means constant speed, and a curve means changing speed.

On a velocity-time graph, the slope equals acceleration, and the area between the line and the time axis equals displacement. A horizontal line means constant velocity. A sloping line means constant acceleration. Area of a rectangle = base × height. Area of a triangle = ½ × base × height.
